messages.subject: Performance difference
parts:
Dear All,

I just found out about this new Bayesian software and it looks really interesting. I am curious about how it compares against WinBUGS or JAGS regarding performance, has anybody tried to run some of the [BUGS examples](http://www.openbugs.net/w/Examples)?

Thanks.

Best,
Shige

messages.author: 0ef2647ddd7095d7
messages.subject: Re: Performance difference
parts:
Hi Shige,

Welcome and thanks for your interest in NIMBLE.

Generally NIMBLE does well in relation to WinBUGS and JAGS. We provide the standard BUGS examples with NIMBLE, although NIMBLE can’t currently handle the ones with indices that are random variables.  The MCMCsuite function (documented in the manual, but let us know if it’s not clear) will automatically run NIMBLE, OpenBUGS and/or JAGS on the same model.  For NIMBLE you can use the default samplers or any custom samplers you set up.  The standard examples can be loaded with readBUGSmodel (again let us know any questions in making that work).  If you’re interested you can look at our automated testing code in inst/tests/test-mcmc.R, which runs over a set of BUGS (and other) models.

I recommend comparing effective sample size per computation time using the effectiveSize function of the coda library.  We have noticed that using conjugate (Gibbs) samplers currently often ends up being less efficient than adaptive random walk samplers (for reasons I could go into but won’t), so you may want to use “useConjugacy = FALSE” in configureMCMC.  We have code to include Stan in MCMCsuite comparisons (using the implementations of the BUGS examples from Stan’s GitHub) and to generate a set of comparison results for any model that we’ll post in the future.  We’ve also been working on high-level control over MCMCs to improve efficiency, such as dynamically assigning block samplers to correlated dimensions.

We are working toward a major release this summer that will have a lot of improvements, especially faster building of models and nimbleFunctions on the R side.

Please let us know questions and share needs or use cases of interest.

Perry

Dear Perry,

Very helpful information, and thanks a lot. I will definitely play with the MCMCsuite function to gain a better understanding.

I also use Stan a lot. One of its weaknesses is its inability of handing dicrete parameters. Since Nimble does not depend on HMC, I assume this should not be a problem here. Am I right?

Best,
Shige

messages.author: 0ef2647ddd7095d7
messages.subject: Re: Performance difference
parts:
Yes that’s correct about discrete parameters.  

In the case that discrete parameters are integers that are latent states used as indices for other parameters, we don’t handle that, but we do plan to and would be happy to hear if anyone is interested in contributing to that.

We do see potential to extend the NIMBLE compiler to generate derivative code and then be able to implement HMC, but we haven’t done that yet, and we’d also be happy to hear if anyone is interested in contributing to that idea.

Cheers,
Perry
